claim: Over 80% of multiple-tested siRNAs and shRNAs targeting CD95 or CD95 ligand (CD95L) induce a form of cell death characterized by simultaneous activation of multiple cell death pathways preferentially killing transformed and cancer stem cells.
source: Over 80% of multiple-tested siRNAs and shRNAs targeting CD95 or CD95 ligand (CD95L) induce a form of cell death characterized by simultaneous activation of multiple cell death pathways preferentially killing transformed and cancer stem cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript, including Figure 1—figure supplement 1 showing toxicity of multiple si/shRNAs, and references to previous work (Hadji et al., 2014).

claim: These si/shRNAs kill cancer cells through canonical RNAi by targeting the 3'UTR of critical survival genes in a unique form of off-target effect called DISE (death induced by survival gene elimination).
source: We now show these si/shRNAs kill cancer cells through canonical RNAi by targeting the 3'UTR of critical survival genes in a unique form of off-target effect we call DISE (death induced by survival gene elimination).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-Seq data (Figure 4), Sylamer analysis (Figure 5A), and multiple experiments demonstrating RNAi mechanism involvement (Figure 3).

claim: Drosha and Dicer-deficient cells, devoid of most miRNAs, are hypersensitive to DISE.
source: Drosha and Dicer-deficient cells, devoid of most miRNAs, are hypersensitive to DISE, suggesting cellular miRNAs protect cells from this form of cell death.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E and 3G comparing wild-type, Dicer-/-, and Drosha-/- HCT116 cells.

claim: Cellular miRNAs protect cells from DISE.
source: Drosha and Dicer-deficient cells, devoid of most miRNAs, are hypersensitive to DISE, suggesting cellular miRNAs protect cells from this form of cell death.
evidence: This is inferred from the hypersensitivity of Drosha-/- and Dicer-/- cells to DISE, which lack most miRNAs.

claim: 4666 shRNAs derived from the CD95 and CD95L mRNA sequences and an unrelated control gene, Venus, were tested.
source: By testing 4666 shRNAs derived from the CD95 and CD95L mRNA sequences and an unrelated control gene, Venus, we have identified many toxic sequences - most of them located in the open reading frame of CD95L.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design shown in Figure 6.

claim: Most toxic sequences are located in the open reading frame of CD95L.
source: By testing 4666 shRNAs derived from the CD95 and CD95L mRNA sequences and an unrelated control gene, Venus, we have identified many toxic sequences - most of them located in the open reading frame of CD95L.
evidence: This is supported by the shRNA screen data shown in Figure 6C and 6D.

claim: Specific toxic RNAi-active sequences present in the genome can kill cancer cells.
source: We propose that specific toxic RNAi-active sequences present in the genome can kill cancer cells.
evidence: This is a proposal based on the collective findings of the study, particularly the shRNA screen and toxicity index analysis.

claim: All five DsiRNAs targeting CD95L displayed toxicity when introduced into HeyA8 cells at 5 nM.
source: All five DsiRNAs displayed toxicity when introduced into HeyA8 cells at 5 nM (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: shL4 was depleted in 99.5% of 216 cell lines tested in a genome-wide analysis.
source: The following shRNAs were found to be depleted in the listed percentage of the 216 cell lines tested: shL4 (99.5%), shL1 (96.8%), shR6 (88.9%), shR7 (75%), shR3 (71.8%), shL2 (67.1%), shR5 (38.4%), shL5 (26.4%), and shR8 (21.3%) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is based on analysis of a published dataset (Cowley et al., 2014).

claim: shL1 was depleted in 96.8% of 216 cell lines tested in a genome-wide analysis.
source: The following shRNAs were found to be depleted in the listed percentage of the 216 cell lines tested: shL4 (99.5%), shL1 (96.8%), shR6 (88.9%), shR7 (75%), shR3 (71.8%), shL2 (67.1%), shR5 (38.4%), shL5 (26.4%), and shR8 (21.3%) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is based on analysis of a published dataset (Cowley et al., 2014).

claim: shR6 was depleted in 88.9% of 216 cell lines tested in a genome-wide analysis.
source: The following shRNAs were found to be depleted in the listed percentage of the 216 cell lines tested: shL4 (99.5%), shL1 (96.8%), shR6 (88.9%), shR7 (75%), shR3 (71.8%), shL2 (67.1%), shR5 (38.4%), shL5 (26.4%), and shR8 (21.3%) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is based on analysis of a published dataset (Cowley et al., 2014).

claim: 67% of tested shRNAs targeting either CD95 or CD95L killed more than half of all tested cancer cell lines.
source: Again in this independent analysis, the majority of tested shRNAs (67%) targeting either CD95 or CD95L killed more than half of all tested cancer cell lines.
evidence: This is based on analysis of a published dataset (Cowley et al., 2014).

claim: A more recent RNAi screen using a second-generation shRNA platform based on a miR-30 backbone did not report toxicity after expressing shRNAs against CD95 or CD95L.
source: Interestingly, a more recent RNAi screen did not report toxicity after expressing shRNAs against CD95 or CD95L (Morgens et al., 2016). The authors of this study used a second-generation shRNA platform based on a miR-30 backbone.
evidence: This is based on a published study (Morgens et al., 2016).

claim: miR-30-based Tet-inducible versions of toxic shRNAs were not highly toxic to HeyA8 cells.
source: To determine the source of the discrepancy in the data, we generated miR-30-based Tet-inducible versions of some of our most toxic shRNAs (shL1, shL3, shL4, shR5, shR6, and shR7, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A) and found none of them to be highly toxic to HeyA8 cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Most miR-30-based shRNAs did not efficiently silence Venus expression.
source: To determine their knockdown efficiency, we induced their expression in cells carrying sensor plasmids in which the fluorophore Venus was linked to either the CD95L or CD95 open reading frame (ORF). Expression of most of these miR-30-based shRNAs also did not efficiently silence Venus expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: shL3 and shR6 expressed in the Tet-inducible pTIP vector killed HeyA8 cells and efficiently suppressed Venus fluorescence.
source: In contrast, two of our most toxic shRNAs shL3 and shR6 when expressed in the Tet-inducible pTIP vector not only killed HeyA8 cells, but also very efficiently suppressed Venus fluorescence in cells expressing the targeted Venus sensor (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D.

claim: The levels of shRNAs produced from the miR-30-based vector may not be sufficient to be toxic to cancer cells.
source: These data suggest that the levels of shRNAs produced from the miR-30-based vector may not be sufficient to be toxic to the cancer cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of toxicity and knockdown efficiency of miR-30-based shRNAs.

claim: Growth of HeyA8 cells was effectively blocked when siL3 was transfected at 1 nM.
source: Growth was effectively blocked (and cells died, data not shown) when siL3 was transfected at 1 nM—a concentration well below the commonly used and recommended siRNA concentration of 5–50 nM)—but not at 0.1 nM.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2E.

claim: Exogenously added recombinant CD95L protein did not protect NB7 cells from the toxicity of CD95L-derived shRNAs.
source: When NB7 cells were incubated with different concentrations of a soluble form of CD95L (S2), toxicity exerted by shL1 was not affected (Figure 1A, left panel).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: NB7 neuroblastoma cells lack expression of caspase-8 and are completely resistant to the apoptosis-inducing effects of CD95L.
source: NB7 neuroblastoma cells were chosen for these experiments because they lack expression of caspase-8 (Teitz et al., 2000) and hence are completely resistant to the apoptosis-inducing effects of CD95L.
evidence: This is based on published literature (Teitz et al., 2000).

claim: Overexpression of shRNA-resistant versions of the CD95L ORF did not protect NB7 cells from shL1 or shL3.
source: Overexpression of these shRNA-resistant versions of the CD95L ORF did not protect the cells from shL1 or shL3, respectively (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Expression of wild-type or mutated CD95 in MCF-7 cells did not reduce the toxicity of shR6 or shR7.
source: Neither expression of wild-type (wt) nor mutated (MUT) CD95 in MCF-7 cells (Figure 1F) reduced the toxicity when cells were infected with the pLKO-shR6 or another toxic lentiviral shRNA, pLKO-shR7 (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F and 1G.

claim: Neither exogenously added recombinant CD95L nor exogenously expressed CD95L or CD95 protein can protect cells from toxic shRNAs derived from these genes.
source: These data suggested that neither exogenously added recombinant CD95L or exogenously expressed CD95L or CD95 protein can protect cells from toxic shRNAs derived from these genes.
evidence: This is inferred from the experiments showing lack of protection by CD95L or CD95 protein.

claim: A 41 nt piece of the CD95L gene containing the target site for shL3 was deleted in 293T cells using CRISPR/Cas9 gene-editing.
source: We first deleted a 41 nt piece of the CD95L gene in 293T cells, that contained the target site for shL3 (Figure 2A and C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and 2C.

claim: 293T shL3 Δ41 cells were equally sensitive to the toxic shRNA shL3 compared to control cells.
source: Compared to a pool of control cells transfected only with the Cas9 plasmid, the 293T shL3 Δ41 cells were equally sensitive to the toxic shRNA (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: HeyA8 cells with homozygous deletion of the shR6 site were still fully toxic to shR6.
source: In all cases, the shRNA or siRNA that targeted the deleted region was still fully toxic to the target-site deleted cells (Figure 2H and I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: HeyA8 cells with homozygous deletion of the siL3 site were still fully toxic to siL3.
source: In all cases, the shRNA or siRNA that targeted the deleted region was still fully toxic to the target-site deleted cells (Figure 2H and I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2I.

claim: Efficient growth reduction and cell death were observed in siL3 site-deleted cells transfected with as little as 1 nM siL3.
source: We saw efficient growth reduction and cell death in siL3 site-deleted cells transfected with as little as 1 nM siL3 (Figure 2I, and data not shown).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2I.

claim: Cells were not dying due to the knockdown of either CD95 or CD95L.
source: These data firmly establish that cells were not dying due to the knockdown of either CD95 or CD95L.
evidence: This is inferred from the experiments showing toxicity in cells with deleted target sites.

claim: Double-stranded siL3 effectively silenced Venus expression and induced toxicity.
source: While double-stranded (ds)-siL3 effectively silenced Venus expression and induced toxicity, neither the sense nor the antisense single-stranded (ss)RNAs significantly decreased Venus expression or induced toxicity (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Single-stranded sense or antisense siL3 RNAs did not significantly decrease Venus expression or induce toxicity.
source: While double-stranded (ds)-siL3 effectively silenced Venus expression and induced toxicity, neither the sense nor the antisense single-stranded (ss)RNAs significantly decreased Venus expression or induced toxicity (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: No activity was found when ds-siL3, synthesized as deoxyribo-oligonucleotides, was transfected into cells.
source: In addition, no activity was found when ds-siL3, synthesized as deoxyribo-oligonucleotides, was transfected into the cells (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Converting siL3 to a blunt-end duplex resulted in substantial loss of RNAi activity and toxicity.
source: Converting siL3 to a blunt-end duplex resulted in substantial loss of RNAi activity and toxicity (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: A 5' modification in the guide strand of siL3 prevented RNAi activity and toxicity.
source: Only when the siL3 duplex carried a 5' modification in the guide strand did it prevent RNAi activity and toxicity; modifications in the three other positions had no effect (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: siL3MUT reduced the growth inhibitory activity of siL3 in a dose-dependent fashion.
source: siL3MUT reduced the growth inhibitory activity of siL3 in a dose-dependent fashion suggesting that siL3 and siL3MUT compete for the same binding site in the cells, pointing at involvement of the RISC.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: siL3 and siL3MUT compete for the same binding site in cells, pointing at involvement of the RISC.
source: siL3MUT reduced the growth inhibitory activity of siL3 in a dose-dependent fashion suggesting that siL3 and siL3MUT compete for the same binding site in the cells, pointing at involvement of the RISC.
evidence: This is inferred from the competition experiment shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Dicer-/- cells were completely resistant to the toxic effects of shL3 or shR6.
source: Consistent with the requirement of Dicer to process shRNAs, Dicer-/- cells were completely resistant to the toxic shRNAs (Figure 3E, center panel).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: shR6 could not silence CD95 protein expression in Dicer-/- cells.
source: This was also supported by the inability of shR6 to silence CD95 protein expression in these cells (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Dicer-/- cells died when transfected with siL3.
source: Dicer-/- cells were not resistant to toxic siRNAs as these cells died when transfected with siL3, which is consistent with mature siRNAs not needing further processing by Dicer (Figure 3G, center panel).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Drosha-/- cells were hypersensitive to the two toxic shRNAs shL3 and shR6.
source: Interestingly, Drosha-/- cells were hypersensitive to the two toxic shRNAs (Figure 3E, right panel, p<0.0001, according to a polynomial fitting model)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: shR6 efficiently knocked down CD95 expression in Drosha-/- cells.
source: and shR6 efficiently knocked down CD95 expression in Drosha-/- cells (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Both Drosha-/- and Dicer-/- cells were much more susceptible to the toxicity induced by siL3 than parental cells.
source: Both Drosha-/- and Dicer-/- cells were much more susceptible to the toxicity induced by siL3 than parental cells (Figure 3G, center and right panel, p<0.0001, according to a polynomial fitting model).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The hypersensitivity of Drosha-/- and Dicer-/- cells to toxic si/shRNAs is explained by more efficient uptake of mature toxic RNAi-active species into the RISC because they are almost completely devoid of competing endogenous miRNAs.
source: The hypersensitivity of the Drosha-/- cells to toxic si/shRNAs and of Dicer-/- cells to toxic siRNAs can be explained by Drosha-/- and Dicer-/- cells allowing much more efficient uptake of mature toxic RNAi-active species into the RISC because they are almost completely devoid of competing endogenous miRNAs (Kim et al., 2016).
evidence: This is inferred from the hypersensitivity data and knowledge about miRNA depletion in these cells (Kim et al., 2016).

claim: The 6mer seed sequence of siL3 was critical for both RNAi activity and its toxicity.
source: These data suggest the 6mer seed sequence of siL3 was critical for both RNAi activity and its toxicity.
evidence: This is inferred from the chimeric siRNA experiments shown in Figure 3H.

claim: One mRNA was upregulated and 11 mRNAs were downregulated in cells treated with toxic shL3 and shR6.
source: The combination of the analyses resulted in one mRNA that was upregulated and 11 mRNAs that were downregulated (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: For nine of the eleven downregulated genes, published data suggest they are either highly upregulated in cancer and/or critical for the survival of cancer cells.
source: Interestingly, for nine of the eleven genes, published data suggest they are either highly upregulated in cancer and/or critical for the survival of cancer cells, as their inhibition or knockdown resulted in either growth reduction or induction of various forms of cell death (see legend of Figure 4—figure supplement 1 for details).
evidence: This is based on published literature cited in the legend of Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Six of the eleven downregulated genes were identified in two independent genome-wide lethality screens to be critical for cancer cell survival.
source: Significantly, six of these eleven downregulated genes were recently identified in two independent genome-wide lethality screens to be critical for cancer cell survival (Blomen et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2015) (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B) (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is based on published genome-wide screens (Blomen et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2015).

claim: There was a significant enrichment (54.5%, p-value=3×10−6) of survival genes among the genes downregulated during DISE.
source: Considering these two screens only identified 6.6% of human genes to be critical for cell survival, we found a significant enrichment (54.5%, p-value=3×10−6 according to binomial distribution) of these survival genes among the genes downregulated during the cell death induced by either shL3 or shR6.
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of the RNA-Seq data compared to published survival gene lists.

claim: All six survival genes downregulated during DISE are either highly amplified or mutated in human cancers.
source: All six survival genes are either highly amplified or mutated in human cancers (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Most of the deregulated mRNAs were downregulated early with a significant effect already at 14 hr, more than two days before the onset of cell death.
source: A kinetic analysis showed most of the deregulated mRNAs were downregulated early with a significant effect already at 14 hr, more than two days before the onset of cell death (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and data not shown).
evidence: This is supported by kinetic qPCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Cells were dying because of the silencing of multiple critical survival genes.
source: This suggested the cells were dying because of the silencing of multiple critical survival genes, providing an explanation for why multiple cell death pathways were activated.
evidence: This is inferred from the RNA-Seq data showing downregulation of multiple survival genes.

claim: Individual knockdown of seven of the eleven downregulated genes resulted in reduced cell growth in HeyA8 cells.
source: Individual knockdown of seven of the targeted genes resulted in reduced cell growth when compared to cells transfected with a pool of scrambled siRNAs (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: 1 nM of a mixture of siRNA pools targeting seven survival genes was sufficient to effectively reduce growth of HeyA8 cells.
source: Remarkably, 1 nM of this siRNA mixture (35.7 pM of each individual siRNA) was sufficient to effectively reduce growth of the cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B) and also cause substantial cell death (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B and 2C.

claim: Survival genes were significantly enriched towards the top of the ranked lists (most downregulated) in all four RNA-Seq data sets.
source: In all cases, survival genes were significantly enriched towards the top of the ranked lists (most downregulated). In contrast, nonsurvival genes were not enriched.
evidence: This is supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Of the 16 genes that were significantly downregulated in cells treated with any of the four sh/siRNAs, 12 were histones.
source: One interesting feature of DISE that emerged was the substantial loss of histones. Of the 16 genes that were significantly downregulated in cells treated with any of the four sh/siRNAs, 12 were histones (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Losing histones is a specific aspect of DISE because the downregulated histones were not the most highly expressed genes in these cells.
source: While it might be expected that dying cells would downregulate highly expressed genes such as histones, we believe that losing histones is a specific aspect of DISE because a detailed analysis revealed the downregulated histones were not the most highly expressed genes in these cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Genes involved in mitotic cell cycle, DNA conformation change, and macromolecular complex assembly were among the most significantly downregulated across all cells in which DISE was induced.
source: A Metascape analysis revealed genes involved in mitotic cell cycle, DNA conformation change, and macromolecular complex assembly were among the most significantly downregulated across all cells in which DISE was induced by any of the four sh/siRNAs (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by Metascape analysis shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Sylamer analysis identified a strong enrichment of the cognate seed match for shL3 and shR6 in cells treated with either of these two shRNAs.
source: This analysis identified a strong enrichment of the cognate seed match for shL3 and shR6 in cells treated with either of these two shRNAs.
evidence: This is supported by Sylamer analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Enrichment in 6mers and 8mers were both detected in the 3'UTRs but not the ORF of the ranked genes.
source: Enrichment in 6mers and 8mers were both detected (only 8mers shown) in the 3'UTRs but not the ORF of the ranked genes (data not shown).
evidence: This is based on Sylamer analysis.

claim: 10 of the 11 downregulated genes identified in the RNA-Seq analysis contained multiple 6mer seed matches for either shL3 and/or shR6.
source: 10 of the 11 downregulated genes identified in the RNA-Seq analysis described in Figure 4A and B contained multiple 6mer seed matches for either shL3 and/or shR6 (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The two shRNAs, shL3 and shR6, killed cells by targeting a network of genes enriched in critical survival genes through RNAi.
source: It is therefore likely the two shRNAs, shL3 and shR6, killed cells by targeting a network of genes enriched in critical survival genes through RNAi.
evidence: This is inferred from the presence of seed matches in survival genes and the RNA-Seq data.

claim: The most abundant mature double-stranded RNAs derived from pLKO-shR6 and pTIP-shL3 were both shifted by one nucleotide from the expected sequence.
source: RNA-Seq analysis performed for the small RNA fraction confirmed in all cases (shScr and shL3 in pTIP, and shScr and shR6 in pLKO), the shRNAs in the cells were cleaved in a way resulting in the predominant formation of an siRNA shifted one nucleotide away from the shRNA loop region (black arrow heads in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by small RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: shRNA-to-siRNA converts of shL3 and shR6 were toxic to HeyA8 cells.
source: These shRNA-to-siRNA converts were toxic to HeyA8 cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B) confirming that the observed toxicity was not limited to the TRC shRNA platform, but based on a sequence-specific activity of the si/shRNAs.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The seed matches of the si/shRNA introduced were significantly enriched in the 3'UTR of downregulated RNAs in cells treated with either shL1 or siL3.
source: In both cases, when the ranked RNA Seq data were subjected to a Sylamer analysis, the seed matches of the si/shRNA introduced were again significantly enriched in the 3'UTR of downregulated RNAs (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by Sylamer analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: In none of the Sylamer analyses of the four data sets was there enrichment of seed matches in the 3'UTRs of downregulated RNAs that matched the passenger strand.
source: In none of the Sylamer analyses of the four data sets, did we see enrichment of seed matches in the 3'UTRs of downregulated RNAs that matched the passenger strand.
evidence: This is based on Sylamer analysis of all four RNA-Seq data sets.

claim: In all Sylamer analyses, the only significantly enriched sequences matched the seed sequences in the guide strand of the si/shRNAs introduced.
source: In all cases, the only significantly enriched sequences matched the seed sequences in the guide strand of the si/shRNAs we introduced.
evidence: This is based on Sylamer analysis of all four RNA-Seq data sets.

claim: shR7 caused downregulation of 7 of 11 of the same genes targeted by shL3 even though the 6mer seed matches of the two shRNAs are very different.
source: While shL1 did not have much of an effect on the expression of these genes, shR7 caused downregulation of 7 of 11 of the same genes targeted by shL3 even though the 6mer seed matches of the two shRNAs are very different (CTTTGT for shL3 and GGAGGA for shR7) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Survival genes containing a predicted seed match in their 3'UTR were statistically more likely to be downregulated than survival genes without such a motif in most cases.
source: In almost all cases, this analysis revealed that survival genes containing a predicted seed match in their 3'UTR were statistically more likely to be downregulated than survival genes without such a motif.
evidence: This is supported by Fisher's Exact test analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The level of knockdown of the targeted genes and the toxicity of shRNAs were not strictly correlated.
source: Now that we had established that the toxicity of the studied shRNAs involved targeting of survival genes rather than CD95 or CD95L, we had to assume that when studying a larger set of shRNAs that the level of knockdown of the targeted genes and the toxicity were not strictly correlated.
evidence: This is inferred from the data and confirmed by experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: Some toxic shRNAs efficiently silenced CD95 while others did not.
source: While some of the toxic shRNAs efficiently silenced CD95 (i.e. shR6 and shR2) few did not (i.e. shR5).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: Cells die by DISE due to an early and selective silencing of survival genes through targeting seed matches in their 3'UTR followed by the downregulation of histones.
source: In summary, our analyses suggest that cells die by DISE due to an early and selective silencing of survival genes through targeting seed matches in their 3'UTR followed by the downregulation of histones.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on all the RNA-Seq and mechanistic data presented.

claim: The pool of 700 shRNAs derived from Venus did not cause any toxicity to NB7 cells.
source: Interestingly, the pool of 700 shRNAs derived from Venus did not cause any toxicity (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The pool of shRNAs derived from CD95L ORF significantly slowed down growth of NB7 cells.
source: In contrast, the pool of the shRNAs derived from CD95L significantly slowed down growth, while no toxicity was observed when cells were infected with the pool of shRNAs derived from the CD95L 3'UTR.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: No toxicity was observed when NB7 cells were infected with the pool of shRNAs derived from the CD95L 3'UTR.
source: In contrast, the pool of the shRNAs derived from CD95L significantly slowed down growth, while no toxicity was observed when cells were infected with the pool of shRNAs derived from the CD95L 3'UTR.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Both the shRNAs derived from the CD95 ORF and the 3'UTR showed some toxicity to NB7 cells.
source: In the case of CD95, both the shRNAs derived from the ORF and the 3'UTR showed some toxicity.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The shRNAs derived from the CD95 3'UTR caused greater toxicity compared to those derived from the ORF.
source: However, the shRNAs derived from the 3'UTR caused greater toxicity compared to those derived from the ORF.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The shRNAs derived from the CD95L ORF and the CD95 3'UTR contain the most toxic sequences overall.
source: The data suggest that overall the shRNAs derived from the CD95L ORF and the CD95 3'UTR contain the most toxic sequences.
evidence: This is inferred from the pooled shRNA toxicity data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The highest enrichment of toxic shRNAs was found amongst those with higher TI for the subpool of shRNAs targeting the CD95L ORF followed by shRNAs in the subpool targeting the CD95 3'UTR.
source: Remarkably, the highest enrichment of toxic shRNAs was found amongst those with higher TI for the subpool of shRNAs targeting the CD95L ORF followed by shRNAs in the subpool targeting the CD95 3'UTR.
evidence: This is supported by the toxicity index analysis shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Survival genes contain more seed matches for toxic shRNAs in their 3'UTR than nonsurvival genes regardless of the expression level.
source: This analysis demonstrates survival genes contain more seed matches for toxic shRNAs in their 3'UTR than nonsurvival genes regardless of the expression level.
evidence: This is supported by the alternative TI analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: It is possible to predict the experimental toxicity of shRNAs based on the in silico calculated TI to a certain extent.
source: This suggests, to a certain extent, it is possible to predict the experimental toxicity of shRNAs based on the in silico calculated TI.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between TI and experimental toxicity shown in Figure 7B.

claim: There was a significant correlation between the GC content of the 6mer seed sequences and higher toxicity of shRNAs detected in the shRNA screen across the CD95L ORF.
source: When the GC content of the 6mer seed sequences of all underrepresented shRNAs detected in the shRNA screen across the CD95L ORF was plotted, we found a significant correlation between the GC content and higher toxicity (indicated by underrepresentation) (Figure 7C and D).
evidence: This is supported by the correlation analysis shown in Figure 7C and 7D.

claim: The correlation between GC content and toxicity was even more pronounced when plotting GC content versus the 6mer toxicity index.
source: This correlation was even more pronounced when plotting GC content versus the 6mer toxicity index (Supplementary file 4) (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is supported by the correlation analysis shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Higher GC content made shRNAs more toxic, consistent with reports demonstrating that shRNAs with high GC content in the seed region showed decreased on-target and increased off-target activity.
source: While not an absolute requirement, higher GC content made shRNAs more toxic, consistent with reports demonstrating that shRNAs with high GC content in the seed region showed decreased on-target and increased off-target activity (Gu et al., 2014; Ui-Tei et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by the correlation data and published literature (Gu et al., 2014; Ui-Tei et al., 2004).

claim: si- and/or shRNAs with certain seed sequences are toxic to cancer cells by targeting critical survival genes through an RNAi mechanism independent of both Drosha and Dicer.
source: In summary, our data suggest that si- and/or shRNAs with certain seed sequences are toxic to cancer cells by targeting critical survival genes through an RNAi mechanism independent of both Drosha and Dicer.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on all the mechanistic and screening data presented.

claim: High miRNA content, presumably through competing for occupancy in the RISC, might render cells less sensitive to DISE.
source: Furthermore, the data suggest high miRNA content, presumably through competing for occupancy in the RISC, might render cells less sensitive to DISE.
evidence: This is inferred from the hypersensitivity of Drosha-/- and Dicer-/- cells which lack miRNAs.

claim: DISE is a unique form of OTE that results in the simultaneous activation of multiple cell death pathways in cancer cells.
source: We now demonstrate DISE is a unique form of OTE that results in the simultaneous activation of multiple cell death pathways in cancer cells.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: The discovery that DISE involves loss of multiple survival genes provides an explanation for the unique properties described for this form of cell death, especially the observation that cancer cells have a hard time developing resistance to this cell death mechanism.
source: The discovery that DISE involves loss of multiple survival genes now provides an explanation for the unique properties we described for this form of cell death, especially the observation that cancer cells have a hard time developing resistance to this cell death mechanism (Hadji et al., 2014; Murmann et al., 2017).
evidence: This is inferred from the findings and supported by previous publications (Hadji et al., 2014; Murmann et al., 2017).

claim: 98.4% of AGO-associated RNAs in HCT116 cells are miRNAs.
source: Using AGO pull-down experiments, we determined 98.4% of AGO- associated RNAs in HCT116 cells to be miRNAs (99.3% in HeyA8 cells, data not shown).
evidence: This is based on AGO pull-down experiments.

claim: Drosha-/- cells showed a reduction of miRNA content from roughly 70–80% to 5–6%.
source: It was recently reported that Drosha-/- cells showed a reduction of miRNA content from roughly 70–80% to 5–6%, and Dicer-/- cells showed a reduction down to 14–21% (Kim et al., 2016).
evidence: This is based on a published study (Kim et al., 2016).

claim: Dicer-/- cells showed a reduction of miRNA content down to 14–21%.
source: It was recently reported that Drosha-/- cells showed a reduction of miRNA content from roughly 70–80% to 5–6%, and Dicer-/- cells showed a reduction down to 14–21% (Kim et al., 2016).
evidence: This is based on a published study (Kim et al., 2016).

claim: Neither Drosha-/- nor Dicer-/- cells express reduced AGO2 protein levels.
source: Since neither Drosha-/- nor Dicer-/- cells express reduced AGO2 protein levels (see inset in Figure 3E), it is reasonable to assume that their RISC can take up many more of the toxic DISE inducing RNAs than the RISC in wt cells explaining the super toxicity of both DISE inducing si/shRNAs and CD95L mRNAs in these cells.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in the inset of Figure 3E.

claim: The RISC in Drosha-/- and Dicer-/- cells can take up many more of the toxic DISE inducing RNAs than the RISC in wt cells, explaining the super toxicity of both DISE inducing si/shRNAs in these cells.
source: Since neither Drosha-/- nor Dicer-/- cells express reduced AGO2 protein levels (see inset in Figure 3E), it is reasonable to assume that their RISC can take up many more of the toxic DISE inducing RNAs than the RISC in wt cells explaining the super toxicity of both DISE inducing si/shRNAs and CD95L mRNAs in these cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the miRNA depletion and AGO2 expression data.

claim: Expression of either shL3 or shR6 induced DISE in immortalized normal ovarian fibroblasts much more efficiently than in matching nonimmortalized cells.
source: We previously showed expression of either shL3 and shR6 induced DISE in immortalized normal ovarian fibroblasts much more efficiently than in matching nonimmortalized cells (Hadji et al., 2014), suggesting that this form of cell death preferentially affects transformed cells.
evidence: This is based on a previous publication (Hadji et al., 2014).

claim: DISE preferentially affects transformed cells.
source: We previously showed expression of either shL3 and shR6 induced DISE in immortalized normal ovarian fibroblasts much more efficiently than in matching nonimmortalized cells (Hadji et al., 2014), suggesting that this form of cell death preferentially affects transformed cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential sensitivity of immortalized vs. non-immortalized cells (Hadji et al., 2014).

claim: Cancer cells in general have global downregulation of miRNAs when compared to normal tissues.
source: It is well documented that cancer cells in general have global downregulation of miRNAs when compared to normal tissues (Lu et al., 2005).
evidence: This is based on published literature (Lu et al., 2005).

claim: Global downregulation of miRNAs in cancer cells might free up the RISC for DISE-inducing RNAs and would imply that miRNAs may protect normal cells from DISE.
source: This might free up the RISC for DISE-inducing RNAs and would imply that miRNAs may protect normal cells from DISE.
evidence: This is inferred from the miRNA downregulation in cancer cells and the hypersensitivity of miRNA-depleted cells to DISE.

claim: Any small RNA with DISE-inducing RNAi activity that does not require Dicer processing can kill cancer cells regardless of Dicer or Drosha status.
source: Overall, our data allow us to predict that any small RNA with DISE-inducing RNAi activity that does not require Dicer processing can kill cancer cells regardless of Dicer or Drosha status.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the findings with siRNAs in Dicer-/- and Drosha-/- cells.

claim: DISE can be triggered in vivo to treat ovarian cancer in mouse xenografts by delivering CD95L-derived siRNAs using nanoparticles.
source: In fact, in an accompanying manuscript, we demonstrate that DISE can be triggered in vivo to treat ovarian cancer in mouse xenografts by delivering CD95L-derived siRNAs using nanoparticles (Murmann et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on an accompanying manuscript (Murmann et al., 2017).

claim: No toxicity was observed in mice treated with CD95L-derived siRNAs using nanoparticles.
source: No toxicity was observed in the treated mice.
evidence: This is based on an accompanying manuscript (Murmann et al., 2017).

claim: It might be possible to develop a novel form of cancer therapy based on the DISE OTE mechanism.
source: These data suggest that it might be possible to develop a novel form of cancer therapy based on the DISE OTE mechanism.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the in vivo findings.
